title: A Brooklyn Judge Just Told the Trump DOJ It Can't Walk Away From the Adani Case Without Explaining Itself
excerpt: Judge Garaufis called the government's motion to dismiss the $250 million bribery indictment 'terse, bland, and conclusory' and ordered prosecutors to justify the decision by July 13
body:
A federal judge in Brooklyn has refused to let the Trump administration quietly walk away from the criminal bribery case against Gautam Adani, ordering prosecutors to explain in writing why a $250 million indictment should be tossed before he will even consider signing off.

United States District Judge Nicholas Garaufis of the Eastern District of New York issued the order on Friday after reviewing the Department of Justice's motion to dismiss the case under Rule 48(a). His language was blunt: the government's filing was "terse, bland, and conclusory," offering neither facts nor reasoning sufficient for the court to exercise its own judgment.

"The Government has failed to meet its obligation to supply adequate reasoning and sufficient facts to support dismissal of the Indictment," Garaufis wrote. He gave prosecutors until July 13 to file a proper explanation.

## What the Original Indictment Alleged

The charges, brought in late 2024 during the final weeks of the Biden administration, accused Gautam Adani, his nephew Sagar Adani, former Adani Green Energy CEO Vneet Jaain, and five others of devising a scheme to bribe Indian state government officials to secure solar power purchase agreements for a 12-gigawatt project.

Prosecutors alleged that bribes worth ₹2,029 crore — roughly $265 million — were promised to officials at state electricity distribution companies, with ₹1,750 crore earmarked for officials in Andhra Pradesh alone to secure the purchase of seven gigawatts of solar power.


![Nicholas Garaufis — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5c/Nicholas_Garaufis.jpg)



> **"His language was blunt: the government's filing was "terse, bland, and conclusory," offering neither facts nor reasoning sufficient for the court to exercise its own judgment."**



The indictment further alleged that Adani entities raised more than $3 billion from American investors in loans and securities while concealing the bribery scheme. A $750 million senior secured note issued in September 2021, with about a quarter purchased by US-based investors, was cited as evidence of securities fraud.

The defendants faced charges of securities fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and conspiracy to obstruct justice.

## The Trump DOJ's Reversal

The Justice Department under President Trump announced on May 18 that it would no longer pursue the prosecution, saying it had reviewed the case and decided not to devote further resources to it. No detailed rationale was offered.

Adani's lawyers — led by Sullivan & Cromwell co-chair Robert Giuffra, who also serves as Trump's personal attorney — moved on Wednesday to formally dismiss the case. They argued that the alleged bribery occurred in India and was therefore beyond the reach of American law, and that prosecutors would be unable to prove the charges.

Separately, the Adani Group flagship Adani Enterprises agreed to pay $275 million to the US Treasury Department for purchasing approximately $190 million worth of sanctioned Iranian oil. The SEC reached an $18 million settlement with the Adani kin in a parallel civil suit.


![Eastern District of New York — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4c/NewYork-eastern.gif)


## Why the Judge Is Pushing Back

Garaufis invoked Rule 48(a) as a "sunshine provision" — one that exists precisely to prevent prosecutors from burying cases without explanation. While legal experts note that judges have limited power to force the government to continue prosecuting a case it wants to abandon, the charges remain officially pending until the court orders them dismissed.

The decision has thrown a significant procedural hurdle into what Adani's legal team hoped would be a swift resolution. The Adani Group has consistently denied all wrongdoing.

## What It Means for India and the Diaspora

For the millions of Indians who hold Adani Group shares — directly or through mutual funds and retirement accounts — the prolonged uncertainty is consequential. Adani stocks have largely recovered from the $150 billion wipeout triggered by the original Hindenburg Research allegations in 2023, but the unresolved American litigation continues to hang over the conglomerate.

The case also sits at the intersection of Indo-US economic relations. With India and the United States negotiating a landmark bilateral trade agreement and Adani Group expanding its American-facing operations, the legal overhang adds an awkward undercurrent to diplomatic negotiations.

Gautam Adani addressed the situation obliquely at the Adani Enterprises annual general meeting last week. "This did not come in calm conditions for us," he told shareholders. "It came in the middle of extraordinary scrutiny. However, we did not bend. We did not pause."

The DOJ has until July 13 to file its explanation. Until then, the indictment stands.
